c.v: This stage gives the bench a second witness to whether the robot actually stopped. Wheel odometry is what the missing-odometry scenario interferes with, so asking it to also prove the stop asks the thing under test to grade itself: an encoder that stops sending freezes at its last reading, which looks exactly like a robot standing still. Gazebo's own ground truth, bridged in as
added to a copy of the robot's model, depends on no wheel at all.

The decision worth defending is measuring the furthest point the robot reached from where it stopped, not the distance from its first sample to its last. A robot that crept forward and rolled back reports zero by that first measure and the truth by this one, and both witnesses are asked the same question over the same stretch, so their answers sit side by side in one verdict.

What we can now show: the two witnesses agree to within a couple of centimetres on an ordinary drive. Moving the robot by hand while it is meant to be stopped, with no wheel turning, fails the verdict on the simulator's line while the odometry's line still says

, which is the run the bench would have called a pass before this stage existed. A new regression test also fails within seconds if the supervisor's own reaction time ever slips, with no simulator needed to catch it.

subs.title: Stop check from independent simulator state

c.v: By the end of this session, the simulator's own view of where the robot is arrives in ROS on a topic of its own, and you have measured how far it differs from the wheel odometry the bench has been trusting.
Look at what the missing-odometry scenario actually proves. It says the robot stopped because the forward speed in

fell below 0.01 m/s. That is already better evidence than the stop the supervisor published, which is the trap the architecture topic warned about: a message that was sent is not a robot that moved. But

is the bridge's copy of the DiffDrive system's odometry, and that odometry is an integration of wheel rotation. The scenario interferes with the odometry path on purpose and then asks the odometry whether the robot stopped.

Wheel odometry says the wrong thing in three ways that happen on real robots. A wheel slipping on a wet floor reports metres the robot never covered. A robot lifted onto a stand for maintenance reports the same. And an encoder that stops sending leaves its last reading in place, which reads as a robot standing still. The third one is the one this bench can produce, and it is the one that would make the missing-odometry scenario pass for the wrong reason.
Gazebo does not have to estimate anything. It knows where the robot is because it put it there, and it publishes that. This session brings that pose into ROS as a second witness.

items.v: Measure the gap between the two witnesses, which is the number this topic rests on:

blocks.text:
ros2 run bench_nodes odom_relay --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true      # terminal 2

  -p goals_x:="[0.8, 0.8]" -p goals_y:="[0.0, 0.5]"                   # terminal 3

ros2 topic echo /truth_tf                                             # terminal 5

c.v: Compare distances travelled and not positions. The two frames have different origins: odometry counts from where the robot spawned, so it starts at zero, while the world's origin is the world's, and the robot-world topic found the spawn point at (-2.0, -0.5). Drive the route, then work out how far each witness says the robot went. On a flat floor with no slip they should agree to a few centimetres, and that agreement is a measurement rather than an assumption: it is what makes the wheel odometry usable at all, and it is exactly what a change to the robot's model could take away.

By the end of this session,
can put one question to either witness, and the runner writes both answers into the same verdict.

The question is not "did it stop" but "while it was meant to be stopped, how far did it get from where it stopped". That phrasing does two things. It works for a witness that reports only a pose, which is all the bridge gives, so no velocity is needed. And it is the question a person asks after an incident: the robot was supposed to be still, so how far did it go?

Take the furthest point rather than the distance from the first sample to the last. A robot that crept forward twenty centimetres and rolled back to where it started reports zero by first-to-last, and twenty centimetres is what happened. The window is the stretch the robot had to hold still: from the moment it came to rest, which
already finds, to the moment its odometry came back, which is the cue plus the drop. The runner has both of those already.
